Reviewed trail 161 at current head `ee7fd888`. One finding remains actionable; three were valid and are now correctly resolved.

- **Medium, open:** `README.json` and `CHANGELOG.xml` still bypass documentation-prefix handling at [`search_file_class.go:410`](https://github.com/entireio/entire-graph/blob/ee7fd888925c52c0ed7f523bba967454a9846759/internal/sem/search_file_class.go#L410). Both receive a `0.5` prior for explicit README/changelog queries and are sectioned away. Keep this finding open.
- **Medium, resolved:** Explicit “update the expected output” requests now use phrase-aware fixture intent. Positive and defect-report cases pass.
- **Medium, resolved:** Annotation parentheses no longer confuse expression-body detection. Annotation, default-argument, and expression-body cases pass.
- **Low, resolved:** Longer plural noun frames now work while singular questions remain guarded.

Focused current-head regressions passed for the three fixes. A temporary test reproduced both remaining failures exactly. No repository or trail state was changed by me.
Why did you keep one finding open?

Because it was still reproducible at `ee7fd888`.

The code treats any recognized extension as non-documentation, including `.json` and `.xml`. Thus `README.json` and `CHANGELOG.xml` become “data” files. Queries such as “update the README” express documentation intent, not data intent, so both files receive a `0.5` ranking prior and can be moved out of primary results.

A temporary regression test confirmed both failures. Unlike the other three findings, no fix or covering test had been added for this case.

I did not change its status myself; I recommended leaving the existing finding open until that behavior is corrected.
Ok, but you can fix it!?

Yes. The defect is narrow and reproducible, so I’ll patch the trail branch, add regression coverage for both `README.json` and `CHANGELOG.xml`, and run the focused search tests. I’ll first use Entire’s current checkout/finding guidance so the work lands on the right trail state.

Trail 161 is now checked out in its own worktree at the latest remote head. Entire also added its worktree directory to the primary checkout’s `.gitignore`; that bookkeeping is unrelated to the fix, so I’ll remove only that generated line before finishing.

content.text: The key design choice is classification, not just the multiplier. I’m keeping prose-named serialized artifacts in the documentation class, while ordinary `settings.json` stays data and `readme_parser.ts` stays source; that keeps classification, ranking intent, sectioning, and the independent documentation prior consistent instead of adding a one-off exception.

One deeper caller changed the choice: reclassifying these files as docs would also trigger a separate `-6` path penalty and could break explicit JSON/XML requests. I’m therefore preserving their accurate `data` taxonomy and adding the missing overlapping documentation-name intent, which fixes ranking and section placement without creating that inverse regression.

The red test reproduces the bug on all three formats: each explicit documentation request gets `0.5` and is moved out of the primary list, while native JSON/XML/YAML intent already behaves correctly. I’m now adding a shared basename predicate and letting the data prior honor documentation intent only when the path itself has a documentation-style name.

The focused test is green, including the existing source-name and explicit-class controls. I’m tightening the helper name to reflect that it deliberately matches prefixes, then I’ll run the broader classifier/section test set and inspect the final diff for unintended scoring changes.

The broader classifier and section tests pass, and `git diff --check` is clean. I’ve handed the two-file diff to independent reviewers and started the full `internal/sem` package suite; while that runs I’ll incorporate any concrete review feedback before committing.

content.text: The implementation stays deliberately narrow: it does not relabel serialized files or weaken their generic-query demotion. It only recognizes the overlap when both facts are present: the file is data, its basename is documentation-shaped, and the query explicitly asks for documentation.

A reviewer caught one real completeness gap before commit: the generic bridge fixes README and CHANGELOG, but canonical names such as `LICENSE.json` are not in the existing documentation-intent vocabulary. I’m extending the check to tie intent to the actual matched basename prefix, then adding LICENSE/CONTRIBUTING controls so “such as” is handled as a class, not just two examples.

That broader LICENSE concern turns out to predate this regression: even plain `LICENSE` is not covered by today’s documentation-intent terms. Expanding it here would change unrelated ranking semantics and could re-promote `CHANGES` files on ordinary “what changes” queries, so I’m keeping this patch scoped to the behavior trail 161 actually regressed.

The final scope is now precise: it restores only the doc-intent behavior lost when recognized data formats began staying in the data class. The full classifier regression set is green; I’m rerunning the complete semantic package on this final diff before committing.

The final diff is two files, whitespace-clean, and the independent review found no actionable issue. The full semantic suite is still exercising the larger search corpus; the branch has not moved underneath us.

The long-running package tests are quiet but healthy, currently around four minutes into their normal ten-minute cap. The targeted regression and all adjacent classifier tests are already green; I’m waiting for the broader result rather than committing ahead of it.

The complete `internal/sem` suite passed: `276.858s`. I’m doing the last remote-head check now; if the trail is still at our base, I’ll commit, push the fix to trail 161, and resolve that exact finding with the verification recorded.
